summary:
Six evals were run (3 iterations each, 30 total, 0 failed). Two of the six ("negative-bedrock-throttling" and "negative-load-balancer-choice") were should_trigger:false negative tests — the trigger correctly fired as expected but all other dimensions were skipped by design, so no comparison data exists for those two.

Across the four substantive evals (hyperpod-application-xid-verdict, gpu-log-coverage-audit, fsx-training-slowdown-cause, preflight-long-run-readiness), a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill tends to meet the expected output more often and pass more assertions, while without_skill is consistently faster and cheaper.

Expected-output match: with_skill hit 3/3 on three of the four evals and 1/3 on gpu-log-coverage-audit; without_skill hit 3/3 only on hyperpod-xid-verdict, and was 0/3 (fsx-training-slowdown-cause), 1/3 (preflight-long-run-readiness), and 0/3 (gpu-log-coverage-audit) elsewhere. Confidence behind these judgments is mostly medium/high, with a few medium-confidence calls, so this is a moderately reliable signal rather than a strong one.

Assertion-level pass rates favor with_skill in 3 of 4 evals (70% vs 70% tied on xid-verdict, 50% vs 31% on gpu-log-coverage, 62% vs 24% on fsx-slowdown, 88% vs 62% on preflight-readiness). Importantly, several individual assertions show no differentiation at all: some always pass for both (e.g., "verdict keyword used," "no raw account ID exposed," "GPU error logging arriving check") and some always fail for both (e.g., "HyperPod health-agent log stream named," "coverage across whole window," "log groups searched," "root cause requires quoted saturation signal," "exact log stream/log group path quoted") — these are either not discriminating between variants or point to a shared gap in both variants' behavior/skill design rather than a difference between them. Where differentiation does occur, it's typically with_skill passing where without_skill fails (e.g., "percentage figures quoted without rescaling," "proven/hypothesis label used verbatim," "deep health checks reported," "per-node coverage reporting") — though on xid-verdict two assertions ("evidence bar for replace verdict," "cause labelled proven/hypothesis") favor without_skill over with_skill, and one assertion pattern is "flaky" in both directions across evals, so the picture is not one-sided.

Runtime and cost consistently favor without_skill: across all four evals, without_skill was faster (e.g., 1m24s vs 3m17s on xid-verdict, 2m32s vs 5m19s on gpu-log-coverage, 1m15s vs 3m21s on preflight-readiness, and more comparably 24m38s vs 26m51s on fsx-slowdown) and cheaper (roughly half the cost in three of four evals). Variant_a also used somewhat more context window in each case, though compaction never occurred for either.

Quality comparison (pairwise LLM judging of outputs) was only available for 2 of the 4 evals (xid-verdict and preflight-readiness) — the other two were fully skipped (0 pairs evaluated for gpu-log-coverage and fsx-slowdown), so quality conclusions are limited. Where available, with_skill was favored more often than without_skill (7 vs 2 on xid-verdict, 3 vs 0 on preflight-readiness), particularly on completeness and accuracy, with actionability roughly split on xid-verdict. Confidence on these quality judgments is medium.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was mixed: both variants were "mostly_consistent" on xid-verdict (identical scores). On fsx-slowdown, with_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.5) while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0), suggesting with_skill's outputs varied more across repeated runs on that eval. Consistency data for without_skill was unavailable (null) on preflight-readiness and for both variants on gpu-log-coverage, limiting how much can be concluded about stability.

Overall, this presents a tradeoff rather than a clear outcome: with_skill shows higher expected-output match, higher assertion pass rates, and higher judged quality in the few evals where quality comparison was possible, at the cost of roughly 2-3x longer runtime and higher spend in most evals; without_skill is substantially faster and cheaper but met the expected output and individual assertions less often in three of the four comparable evals, and showed a quality edge nowhere where quality was measured. Several assertions and one full eval dimension (quality) had too little or no data to differentiate the variants, and some findings rest on medium or low confidence judgments, so these differences should be read as directional rather than definitive.

hyperpod-application-xid-verdict.summary:
Both variants fired the trigger behavior in all 3/3 runs and met the overall expected output in 3/3 runs each, with high-confidence judgments — so on the top-line "did it meet expectations" measure, the two variants are tied.

Per-assertion detail (30 assertions total, both at 70% aggregate) shows the tie masks real differences underneath:
- Several assertions pass for both variants in all runs (verdict keyword used, Xid code quoted, no raw account ID exposed) — these aren't discriminating between the variants.
- One assertion (naming the HyperPod health-agent log stream) fails for both variants in all runs — this looks like a capability gap or an assertion/behavior mismatch that neither variant satisfies, not a point of difference.
- Where the variants diverge: without_skill did notably better on stating the evidence bar for a replace verdict (3/3 vs 1/3) and on labeling causes as proven vs. hypothesis (3/3 vs 2/3). with_skill did notably better on reporting whether HyperPod itself took recovery action (3/3 vs 2/3) and on naming the affected instance ID (3/3 vs 2/3). Both were weak and roughly similar on naming the log group/stream for Xid evidence (with_skill 1/3, without_skill 0/3). Many of these are flagged as "flaky" patterns, meaning results varied across the 3 repeated runs for each variant, so single-run differences should be read cautiously.

On independent LLM-judged quality comparisons (3 pairs evaluated, medium confidence), with_skill was favored more often overall (7 of 10 criterion-level comparisons) versus without_skill (2 of 10), with 1 comparable. Breaking that down: with_skill was favored on completeness in all 3 pairs and on accuracy in 2 of 3 (1 comparable), while actionability was split evenly (2 with_skill vs 2 without_skill across the criterion instances). This is a fairly small sample (3 pairs) and medium confidence, so the magnitude should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

On efficiency, without_skill was substantially faster (avg 1m24s vs 3m17s for with_skill) and cheaper (avg $0.70 vs $1.64), with lower context utilization (3.9% vs 6.6%); neither showed any compaction events. All runs for both variants exceeded the 30-second runtime threshold used for comparison, so this check didn't distinguish them beyond confirming both run well over that bar.

Output consistency across repeated runs was identical for both variants: "mostly_consistent" overall with the same score (2.67) and the same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly_consistent), at high confidence — so neither variant showed more run-to-run stability than the other.

Overall, this is a tradeoff pattern rather than a clear separation: without_skill is markedly faster and cheaper and edges out with_skill on two specific assertions (evidence-bar articulation, cause confidence-labeling), while with_skill is favored more often in holistic quality comparisons (particularly completeness) and edges out without_skill on two other assertions (recovery-action reporting, instance ID naming). Both variants share the same weaknesses (log stream naming assertion fails for both) and the same consistency profile. Given the small sample sizes (3 runs/pairs) and several flaky/medium-confidence results, these differences should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

gpu-log-coverage-audit.summary:
This single chat-task eval examined how the two agent variants investigate kernel/Xid error reporting across cluster nodes.

Trigger and basic firing: the behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3), so there's complete data to evaluate on.

Expected output match: both variants struggled, but with_skill met the expected output more often (1/3, 33%) than without_skill (0/3, 0%). Confidence in these expected-output judgments is only medium (not low, but not high either), so this gap should be read as a real but not strongly certain signal.

Per-assertion detail (8 distinct assertions, with_skill run once per assertion vs without_skill run twice, giving without_skill double the sample count):
- Two assertions passed consistently for both variants ("establishes whether kernel logging was arriving before concluding on Xid errors" and "distinguishes no-errors-found from non-observable evidence") — these aren't differentiating since both pass.
- One assertion ("coverage reported per node, not as a blanket cluster statement") clearly separated the two: with_skill passed 1/1 while without_skill failed 0/2.
- Three assertions failed for both variants entirely: establishing coverage across the whole window (with_skill 0/1 with low confidence, without_skill 0/2), reporting which log groups were searched (both 0), and quoting a full log group path (both 0) and an exact log stream name (both 0). These point to shared weaknesses in both agents or to assertions that may be set up too strictly, rather than a difference between variants.
- One regex assertion ("at least two compute node instance IDs examined") was flaky for without_skill (1/2) while with_skill passed its single run (1/1) — too little data to call this a stable difference.

Aggregate assertion pass rates were 4/8 (50%) for with_skill vs 5/16 (31%) for without_skill, driven mostly by the per-node-coverage assertion and the smaller sample for with_skill (1 run per assertion vs 2), so this aggregate should be read cautiously.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (2m32s vs 5m19s) and cheaper ($1.27 vs $2.65) than with_skill, with lower context-window utilization (4.0% vs 5.6%) and no compactions for either. This is a clear efficiency difference in favor of without_skill, but it coincides with without_skill doing less well on expected-output match and on the per-node-coverage assertion — a tradeoff between speed/cost and some correctness measures rather than a one-sided result.

Quality comparison and consistency: no quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), and output-consistency-across-runs is null for both variants, so neither dimension offers usable evidence here.

Overall, the data suggests with_skill more often satisfied the expected output and the per-node-coverage assertion, while without_skill ran faster and cheaper; several assertions (coverage across full window, log group reporting, exact log group/stream quoting) failed for both variants, indicating shared gaps rather than a variant-specific issue. Sample sizes are small (3 runs total) and several judgments rest on medium or low confidence, so these findings should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Both variants reliably triggered the behavior under test (3/3), so the eval setup itself worked for both.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, medium confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (high confidence in that judgment). This is a large, clearly-measured gap, though it rests on only 3 task runs, which limits statistical certainty despite the confidence label.

Per-assertion detail (21 assertion-checks across 7 unique assertions, 3 runs each):
- One assertion ("nothing is called the root cause unless a measured saturation signal is quoted") failed for both variants in all runs — this indicates either a genuinely hard requirement neither agent satisfies, or an assertion that may need rework, rather than a point against either variant specifically.
- Two assertions ("names the specific measurement to confirm/reject the hypothesis" and "signals that could not be read are reported as not observable") passed at the same rate for both variants (2/3 each), so they don't differentiate the variants, though both are flagged as "flaky" (inconsistent across repeated runs for at least one variant).
- One assertion ("FSx file system is identified") passed 1/3 for both variants — identical but low pass rate, also flagged flaky.
- Two assertions showed a clear split in favor of with_skill: quoting FSx/GPU percentages without rescaling (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 0/3, though without_skill's confidence here was low) and using a proven/hypothesis label verbatim (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 0/3, this one a deterministic regex check, so more trustworthy).
- One assertion (explicit proven/hypothesis labeling) also favored with_skill (2/3 vs 0/3) but is marked flaky.
Overall assertion pass rate was 62% for with_skill vs 24% for without_skill, consistent with the expected-output gap, but several individual assertions show no difference or flakiness, meaning the aggregate gap is driven by a subset of checks rather than uniform superiority.

Quality comparison: no pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available between the variants.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran about 2m13s longer (26m51s vs 24m38s) and cost about $1.11 more on average ($13.38 vs $12.27) than without_skill. Variant_b also used more context window (61.1% vs 45.5%); neither showed any compaction events.

Output consistency across repeated runs: without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, all 4 dimensions mostly consistent, medium confidence), while with_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.5, 2 of 4 dimensions inconsistent, high confidence). This suggests with_skill's outputs varied more run-to-run even though it passed more assertions and met the expected output more often on average.

Net picture: with_skill shows a substantially higher rate of meeting the expected output and a higher overall assertion pass rate, with two assertions (one regex-based, more reliable) clearly favoring it. However, this comes alongside somewhat higher runtime/cost, greater run-to-run inconsistency, and no available head-to-head quality comparison. One assertion fails for both variants outright, and several others show identical or flaky results that don't differentiate the two. The expected-output and per-assertion gap is the most notable finding, but it should be weighed against the small sample size (3 runs), the inconsistency finding for with_skill, and the lack of quality-pair data.

preflight-long-run-readiness.summary:
This eval tested a chat-based AWS DevOps readiness-check scenario (SageMaker HyperPod cluster review) with 3 runs per variant. The trigger behavior fired in all cases (3/3), so both variants were properly exercised.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 1 of 3 runs (33%, medium confidence). This is the clearest signal in the data, though without_skill's lower confidence rating means that measurement itself is somewhat less certain.

Per-assertion pass rates: with_skill passed 21/24 (88%) vs without_skill's 10/16 (62%) — note the different denominators reflect fewer total assertions evaluated for without_skill. Looking at individual assertions:
- Two assertions passed for both variants on every run ("checks not verified are reported as unverified" and "the cluster is named") — these aren't distinguishing the variants.
- One assertion ("deep health checks enabled is reported") passed 100% for with_skill but 0% for without_skill — a clear divergence.
- Several assertions are flagged "flaky" for one or both variants (reserved capacity comparison, GPU error logging as readiness item, individual check reporting, node recovery setting, per-check result keyword), meaning results varied across runs rather than being stable one way or the other. Notably, on "checks reported individually" and "per-check result keyword," without_skill actually scored equal or higher than with_skill, showing the pattern isn't uniformly in with_skill's favor.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 task pairs could actually be evaluated for quality (2 were skipped), so this is a thin sample. In that one comparable pair, with_skill was favored on accuracy and actionability, with completeness rated comparable; confidence in this comparison is medium.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was notably faster (1m15s vs 3m21s) and cheaper (~$0.62 vs ~$1.67), with lower context window utilization (4.0% vs 6.5%). Only one runtime pair was evaluated against the 30s threshold, and that one run exceeded it (likely with_skill given its longer average runtime, though the threshold data isn't broken out by variant here).

Output consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly consistent" across its runs (score 2.0, high confidence). No consistency rating is available for without_skill (null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's absent data, not a sign of inconsistency.

Overall, the strongest and most confident finding is that with_skill met the expected output and most assertions more reliably than without_skill, including one assertion where without_skill failed outright. However, this comes with a real tradeoff: with_skill took roughly 2x longer and cost over 2.5x more than without_skill. The quality-comparison and runtime-threshold findings rest on very small samples (1 pair each), and several assertions showed flaky, run-to-run variation for one or both variants, so some of these differences should be read as directional rather than firmly established.
